skill.name: wp-performance
skill.description: Investigate and improve WordPress backend performance with WP-CLI, Server-Timing, Query Monitor data, and safe verification steps.
skill.summary: Diagnose WordPress performance bottlenecks with backend-focused measurements and repeatable checks.
skill.author: Automattic

security_audit.summary: Most static findings are documentation examples, benign WordPress performance guidance, or false matches on JavaScript template literals. The only confirmed risk is the helper script invoking WP-CLI through child_process, which is legitimate but should require clear user approval because WP-CLI can execute local WordPress code.

remediation.issue: Helper script executes WP-CLI through child_process.
remediation.suggestion: Keep the no-shell spawnSync pattern, but document that running the script executes WP-CLI against the selected WordPress install and requires explicit user approval.

remediation.issue: User-supplied --path and --url determine the WordPress target.
remediation.suggestion: Recommend running only against trusted local or staging installs, and show the exact WP-CLI commands before execution when used by an agent.

content.value_statement: Slow WordPress sites are hard to diagnose without repeatable backend measurements. This skill guides Claude, Codex, and Claude Code through WP-CLI checks, profiling, and safe verification.
actual_capabilities: Builds a backend-only WordPress performance investigation plan.
Runs or recommends WP-CLI doctor and profile checks when available.
Inspects autoloaded options size and cache drop-in presence with the helper script.
Guides Query Monitor and Server-Timing analysis without a browser UI.
Maps bottlenecks to database, cache, cron, HTTP API, or theme resource fixes.
Defines verification steps using the same target URL, route, and environment.
limitations: Requires WP-CLI access for the strongest diagnostics.
Does not replace production load testing or full APM traces.
Cannot safely install plugins, flush caches, or enable debug tooling without approval.
Backend measurements may not capture all client-side performance problems.

use_cases.title: Investigate slow page loads
use_cases.description: Measure backend timing, profile WP-CLI stages, and identify the dominant bottleneck before changing code.

use_cases.title: Audit production readiness
use_cases.description: Use WP-CLI doctor guidance to find autoload bloat, debug flags, cron issues, and other performance risks.

use_cases.title: Plan safe optimization work
use_cases.description: Choose focused fixes for queries, caching, cron, or remote HTTP calls and verify results with repeatable measurements.

prompt_templates.title: Start a basic performance check
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner investigation for a slow WordPress page.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the wp-performance skill to investigate a slow WordPress page. My environment is staging, the WP root is <path>, and the slow URL is <url>. Start with safe read-only checks.

prompt_templates.title: Analyze WP-CLI diagnostic output
prompt_templates.scenario: Review existing command output before deciding fixes.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the wp-performance skill to interpret this wp doctor and wp profile output. Identify the likely bottleneck, the evidence, and the safest next measurement.

prompt_templates.title: Optimize a specific bottleneck
prompt_templates.scenario: Focus on one confirmed performance category.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the wp-performance skill for a database bottleneck. Review the query symptoms, suggest low-risk changes, and define how to verify query count and TTFB improvement.

prompt_templates.title: Create a production-safe rollout plan
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced planning for a sensitive production site.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the wp-performance skill to create a production-safe optimization plan. Include approval gates, read-only diagnostics, staging validation, rollout steps, and rollback criteria.

output_examples.input: A staging WordPress site has high TTFB on one product page.
output_examples.output: The skill produces a baseline plan, WP-CLI checks, likely bottleneck categories, and a verification checklist for the same URL.

output_examples.input: WP-CLI doctor reports large autoloaded options and debug settings enabled.
output_examples.output: The skill explains the performance impact, ranks the issues, and recommends safe changes before repeating the diagnostic checks.

output_examples.input: Query Monitor headers show slow remote HTTP calls during REST requests.
output_examples.output: The skill suggests timeouts, caching, batching, or async processing, then defines measurements to confirm lower latency.

best_practices: Capture a baseline before changing code or configuration.
Run risky operations only after explicit approval in the target environment.
Verify improvements with the same URL, route, cache state, and environment.
anti_patterns: Do not flush caches in production as a first troubleshooting step.
Do not enable SAVEQUERIES or profiling plugins in production without approval.
Do not optimize multiple bottleneck categories at once before measuring impact.

faq.question: Does this skill require browser access?
faq.answer: No. It is designed for backend-only WordPress diagnostics using WP-CLI, logs, HTTP headers, and REST responses.

faq.question: Can it run WP-CLI commands?
faq.answer: Yes, the helper script can invoke WP-CLI when the user approves execution in the target environment.

faq.question: Is it safe for production sites?
faq.answer: It can guide read-only production diagnostics, but write operations, plugin installs, cache flushes, and load tests need explicit approval.

faq.question: What performance areas does it cover?
faq.answer: It covers backend timing, database queries, autoloaded options, object caching, cron, remote HTTP calls, and verification.

faq.question: Does it fix code automatically?
faq.answer: No. It helps identify likely fixes and verification steps. Implementation still depends on the WordPress project and user approval.

faq.question: Can it use Query Monitor without a browser?
faq.answer: Yes. It describes how to inspect Query Monitor data through REST headers and envelope responses when configured.
